qs.q: A patient with long-standing mitral stenosis develops a massive left atrial enlargement. Upon clinical examination, the patient is noted to have a hoarse voice and difficulty swallowing. What is the direct anatomical cause of these specific findings?
o: Compression of the recurrent laryngeal nerve and esophagus by the massively enlarged left atrium
Direct infiltration of the vagus nerve by bacterial antibodies during an episode of acute rheumatic fever
Stenosis of the pulmonary veins causing localized edema around the vocal cords and surrounding pharynx
Compression of the trachea and mainstem bronchi by a severely hypertrophied left ventricular wall
qs.e: Massive left enlargement of the left atrium in mitral stenosis can mechanically compress the recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness, and the esophagus, causing dysphagia. The left ventricle is actually normal or small in pure mitral stenosis.

qs.q: A 45-year-old female presents with progressive dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and palpitations. Physical examination reveals a loud S1, an opening snap, and a mid-diastolic rumble. Which radiographic finding is most consistent with pure mitral stenosis?
o: Prominent left ventricular enlargement with apical displacement and signs of strain
Right ventricular atrophy accompanied by entirely normal pulmonary vasculature
Enlarged left atrium with a normal left ventricular size and normal shape
Significant cardiomegaly driven purely by progressive right atrial dilation
qs.e: In pure mitral stenosis, the left ventricle remains normal or small in size, while the left atrium becomes massively enlarged. Left ventricular enlargement is characteristic of aortic or mitral regurgitation.

qs.q: A 60-year-old patient presents with signs of systemic embolization, having suffered a transient ischemic attack. Echocardiography shows severe left atrial dilation and stagnant blood flow within the left atrial appendage. Which arrhythmia commonly arises from left atrial stretching in mitral stenosis and promotes thrombus formation?
o: Atrial fibrillation arising from left atrial stretching
Ventricular tachycardia stemming from left ventricular strain
First-degree AV block caused by progressive nodal fibrosis
Sinus bradycardia resulting from altered pacemaker function
qs.e: Stretching and dilation of the left atrium disrupt its electrical pathways, frequently resulting in atrial fibrillation, stasis of blood, and thrombus formation. Ventricular arrhythmias do not stem directly from left atrial enlargement.

qs.q: When does a patient with mitral stenosis typically begin to experience symptoms according to the normal valve area measurements?
o: When the MV area is between 4-6 cm2
When the MV area drops below 2 cm2
When the MV area is exactly 3.5 cm2
When the MV area exceeds 6 cm2
qs.e: The normal mitral valve area is 4-6 cm2, and symptoms begin when the valve area drops to less than 2 cm2. A mild mitral stenosis is considered when the orifice is reduced to approximately 2 cm2.

qs.q: A patient with severe mitral stenosis presents with hoarseness of voice. What is the most likely pathophysiological mechanism for this symptom?
o: Direct compression of the trachea by pulmonary edema
Impingement of an enlarged left atrium on the recurrent laryngeal nerve
Left ventricular hypertrophy compressing the vagus nerve
Pulmonary hypertension causing vocal cord paralysis
qs.e: Hoarseness in mitral stenosis is due to the impingement of an enlarged left atrium on the recurrent laryngeal nerve. It is one of the distinct symptoms associated with severe left atrial enlargement.

qs.q: Which physical examination finding is classically associated with mitral stenosis?
o: A wide pulse pressure with a diastolic decrescendo murmur
An opening snap followed by a low-pitched diastolic rumble
A holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla with an S3 gallop
A harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur
qs.e: Mitral stenosis characteristically presents with an opening snap followed by a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble due to turbulent blood flow. A wide pulse pressure and diastolic decrescendo murmur are characteristic of aortic regurgitation.

qs.q: What is the primary test of choice for diagnosing and evaluating mitral stenosis?
o: Electrocardiography (ECG)
Chest radiography
Echocardiography (Echo 2D/color doppler)
Cardiac catheterization
qs.e: Echocardiography (2D/color doppler) is the test of choice for diagnosing mitral stenosis. ECG is helpful for rhythm assessment but is not diagnostic on its own.

qs.q: A patient with non-calcified, pliable mitral stenosis undergoes a catheter-based procedure to treat the underlying cause. Which of the following treatments was most likely performed?
o: Percutaneous Balloon Valvuloplasty
Mitral Valve Replacement
Open Commissurotomy
Diuretic administration
qs.e: Percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty is the surgical therapy used for non-calcified, pliable valves via a catheter. Mitral valve replacement is reserved for when a catheter procedure cannot be done.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Mitral stenosis is a rheumatic valve disease that narrows the mitral orifice, impeding left‑ventricular filling and causing pulmonary hypertension and atrial fibrillation. It presents with exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and a characteristic opening snap and mid‑diastolic rumble.

sections.p: Mitral stenosis is a fixed obstruction of the mitral valve opening, most often due to rheumatic fever. Diagnosis relies on auscultation, echocardiography, and clinical context.

t.b: Measures mitral valve area and pressure gradient; a valve area <1.5 cm² confirms stenosis and grades severity.
Shows left atrial enlargement and pulmonary vascular congestion; useful when echo unavailable.
Detects atrial fibrillation or left atrial enlargement; not diagnostic alone.

sections.p: Severity is staged by valve area and mean gradient, guiding treatment urgency.

t.b: >10 mmHg indicates severe stenosis; correlates with symptoms.

sections.p: Rheumatic fever is the leading cause worldwide, especially in low‑resource settings. Other causes include congenital stenosis and calcific degeneration in the elderly.

t.b: Genetic susceptibility to rheumatic fever; explains regional prevalence.

sections.p: Patients develop exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and cough. A loud first heart sound, opening snap, and mid‑diastolic rumble are classic auscultatory findings.

t.b: Occurs 150–200 ms after S1; indicates valve leaflet thickening.
Best heard at apex in left lateral decubitus; reflects turbulent flow.

sections.p: Echocardiography is the gold standard. When unavailable, chest X‑ray and ECG guide suspicion.

t.b: Assesses valve area, gradient, and left atrial size; confirms diagnosis.
Shows left atrial enlargement and pulmonary congestion; supports clinical suspicion.
Detects atrial fibrillation or left atrial enlargement; prompts anticoagulation.

sections.p: Complications include atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension, hemoptysis, and systemic emboli. Red flags are sudden worsening dyspnea, hemoptysis, or new atrial fibrillation.

t.b: May indicate pulmonary edema or tamponade; urgent evaluation needed.

sections.p: Treat the underlying rheumatic process, control symptoms, and prevent complications. Definitive therapy is percutaneous balloon valvotomy or surgery.

t.b: Prevents systemic emboli in AF; warfarin is preferred in rheumatic disease.
Reduce pulmonary congestion; avoid over‑diuresis that lowers preload.
Relieves obstruction; chosen when valve area <1.5 cm² and patient is symptomatic.

sections.p: Regular echocardiographic monitoring, vaccination against streptococcal infection, and early treatment of sore throats reduce recurrence.

t.b: Tracks valve area and pulmonary pressures; guides timing of intervention.
Prevents recurrent rheumatic fever; reduces progression of stenosis.

sections.p: Mitral regurgitation, pulmonary hypertension, and left ventricular failure can mimic mitral stenosis symptoms.
b: Mitral regurgitation – holosystolic murmur, not opening snap
Pulmonary hypertension – loud S2, not mid‑diastolic rumble
LV failure – S3 gallop, not opening snap

sections.p: A normal chest X‑ray can occur in early disease; a normal ECG may miss silent atrial fibrillation.
b: Early disease may show normal imaging
Silent AF can be missed on ECG

Paroxysmal AF may be missed; consider Holter monitoring in symptomatic patients.

faq.q: Why is the left ventricle protected in mitral stenosis?
faq.a: Because the obstruction limits preload, the left ventricle does not experience volume overload.
The valve cannot be reversed, but percutaneous balloon valvotomy or surgery can relieve obstruction and improve symptoms.

faq.q: Is anticoagulation needed in all patients?
faq.a: Only in those with atrial fibrillation or left atrial thrombus; otherwise not routinely indicated.
